title: The Undertow of the reservoir
premise: Tamsin Marchetti, a translator raised bilingual in a village drowned by the Ashcombe Reservoir, has spent a decade in London letting their mother's dialect slip away word by word—until a box of forty-year-old undelivered letters, hidden behind a wardrobe inherited from their grandmother, reveals that the village's flooding was engineered through fraud by the family whose name Tamsin now translates for. The letters, written in the dying dialect by villagers who were never told the truth, implicate Tamsin's own grandfather as the surveyor whose false readings condemned the valley. As Tamsin translates the letters toward the one untranslatable sentence—the dying confession of the village postman—powerful descendants of the water company move to bury the documents and the translator alike. In the end, Tamsin publishes the translation not as accusation but as elegy, reads the untranslatable sentence aloud at the reservoir's edge in a dialect only three living people can still hear, and accepts that justice outside the law arrives as memory made public, not as restitution.
about_author: U. M. Crane is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up in a valley now under water and has published two collections of translated folk songs. They write from a houseboat on a reservoir, where they claim the drowned village sends up its vocabulary in bubbles.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In London, Tamsin translates a developer's glossy brochure and realizes they no longer remember the dialect word for 'heron.' A solicitor's letter announces their grandmother's death and an inheritance in the drowned valley. Emotional beat: the quiet grief of losing a language and a homeland simultaneously, disguised as professional detachment.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Returning to Ashcombe, Tamsin clears the flooded-era cottage and finds the wardrobe too heavy to move; behind it, a tin box of letters, all addressed but never posted, all in dialect. The postmark date is three days before the flooding order. Emotional beat: dread and fascination—the past refusing to stay submerged.

chapters.title: Letters Without Addresses
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, interleaved with the letters themselves. The first letters describe small village life, then a surveyor's visit, then rising fear. Tamsin recognizes their grandfather's handwriting on one envelope as the recipient. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering your family on the wrong side of someone else's catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Surveyor's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Edith Marchetti's letters, 1983. She loved the surveyor's daughter, Tamsin's mother, and wrote to her for years; every letter was returned unopened. Through her, we see the fraud: readings altered, compensation lists falsified, the valley condemned on paper before it was drowned. Emotional beat: love thwarted by complicity, inheritance as guilt.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin tracks down the surveyor's daughter—their own mother—now in a care home, her dialect nearly gone. She recognizes one word of the letters and weeps without knowing why. Tamsin cannot bring themselves to ask the question. Emotional beat: tenderness and cowardice, the art of almost saying it practiced one more day.

chapters.title: The Company of Descendants
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A local archivist, Ruth, helps authenticate the letters, and word spreads. A lawyer representing Halliwell Water—now a private equity firm—visits with an offer: sell the letters, sign an NDA, generous terms. Tamsin hesitates, needing money and afraid of the fight. Emotional beat: the seduction of silence, power offering a comfortable shape to corruption.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Near the bottom of the box, the postman's last letter contains a sentence Tamsin cannot render: it names the grandfather directly and asks not for punishment but for the valley's name to be spoken aloud. Every English word Tamsin tries is a betrayal. Emotional beat: the translator's crisis—fidelity to a sentence that demands the translator's own ruin or redemption.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The firm escalates: the archive's funding is cut, Ruth is dismissed, and Tamsin's translation clients quietly drop them. Tamsin nearly burns the letters in the cottage hearth. Ruth finds the ashes unlit and the letters intact, and for the first time says aloud what Tamsin has avoided: publish it. Emotional beat: the moment fear tips into resolve.

chapters.title: The Sentence Spoken
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Climax. At a hearing Tamsin was never meant to survive, the firm's lawyer produces Tamsin's grandfather's sealed survey, proving nothing new—only that everyone always knew. Tamsin abandons the prepared legal statement and instead reads the postman's letter in the original dialect, ending on the untranslatable sentence, untranslated, in a room that does not understand the words but understands everything. Emotional beat: justice as witness; the sentence lands like water finding its level.

chapters.title: What the Heron Knows
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, a year later. The letters are published as a small book no bestseller list notices, but the village's descendants gather each spring at the reservoir's edge to read them aloud. Tamsin's mother, in her last lucid hour, says the heron word. Tamsin teaches it to Ruth's daughter. Emotional beat: inheritance transformed—what was stolen is not returned, but what was almost said is finally said, and carried forward.
